JUDGEMENT
PER HON’BLE MR. AJAY TALEGAONKAR, TECHNICAL MEMBER
1. The present Appeal has been filed by the Appellant Damodar Valley Power
Consumers’ Association (“DVPCA”) and its members challenging the Impugned
Order dated 31.03.2025 passed by the West Bengal Electricity Regulatory
Commission (“WBERC”/ “Respondent No. 1”/ “State Commission”) in Case No.
APR-125/ 24-25 whereby the State Commission had undertaken Annual
Performance Review (APR) for FY 2021-22 in respect of retail supply of electricity
by Damodar Valley Corporation (“DVC”/ “Respondent No. 2”) within its command
area in the State of West Bengal.
Page 6 of 41

Judgement in Appeal No. 15 of 2026
Description of the Parties
2. The Appellant No. 1, DVPCA is a company incorporated under Section 8 of
the Companies Act, 1956 and is a collective body representing the interests of its
members who are HT consumers of DVC.
3. The Appellant Nos. 2 to 32 are industrial consumers of DVC and are also
members of the Appellant No. 1.
4. Respondent No. 1, WBERC is a statutory body under Section 82 of the
Electricity Act, 2003. The State Commission is entrusted, inter alia, with the
function of determination of tariff for retail supply of tariff within the State of West
Bengal.
5. Respondent No. 2, DVC is a statutory corporation owned and controlled by
the Government of India, Government of Jharkhand and Government of West
Bengal and is engaged in generation, transmission, bulk-supply and distribution of
electricity and performs diverse functions relating to irrigation, flood control,
afforestation, soil conservation etc. in accordance with the provisions of the DVC
Act. However, in matters of tariff determination, DVC is governed by the provisions
of the Electricity Act, 2003. The power distribution activity of DVC is confined to
industrial HT consumers, receiving power at 33 KV and above in its command area
falling in the States of West Bengal and Jharkhand. The members of the Appellant
Association i.e. Appellant Nos. 2 to 32 are HT/ EHT consumer of DVC, having their
manufacturing facility in the State of West Bengal.
Factual Matrix of the Case
6. The State Commission notified the WBERC (Terms and Conditions of Tariff)
Regulations, 2011 governing tariff determination in the State of West Bengal. The
Page 7 of 41

Judgement in Appeal No. 15 of 2026
Central Electricity Regulatory Commission (“CERC”) notified the CERC (Terms
and Conditions of Tariff) Regulations, 2014 for the control period FY 2014-19 and
thereafter notified the CERC (Terms and Conditions of Tariff) Regulations, 2019
for the control period FY 2019-24.
7. Pursuant thereto, the State Commission passed several Aggregate Revenue
Requirement (“ARR”), tariff and APR orders concerning DVC for different control
periods.
8. For the period FY 2014-17, the State Commission passed an ARR Order
dated 25.05.2015 and subsequently an APR Order dated 08.06.2023.
9. For FY 2021-22, the Annual Fixed Charges (“AFC”) pertaining to various
generating stations as well as the Transmission and Distribution (“T&D”) system
of DVC were determined by the CERC through tariff orders issued for the control
period FY 2019-24.
10. DVC filed a tariff petition on 26.02.2020 for determination of tariff for FY
2020-23. Thereafter, by ARR Order dated 07.03.2024, the State Commission
determined the retail tariff applicable to DVC for FY 2020-23. In relation to FY
2021-22, DVC filed an APR Petition dated 28.06.2024 before the State
Commission on 01.07.2024.
11. DVC had earlier filed review petitions against the APR Orders dated
18.09.2023, 11.12.2023 and 11.01.2024 pertaining respectively to FY 2017-18, FY
2018-19 and FY 2019-20. By separate review orders dated 24.03.2025, the State
Commission reviewed the aforesaid APR Orders.
Page 8 of 41

Judgement in Appeal No. 15 of 2026
12. While passing the said review orders, the State Commission adopted an
“empirical formula” proposed by DVC for computation of interest on differential
AFC.
13. The same empirical formula was also applied by the State Commission in
relation to FY 2014-17. Thereafter, the State Commission passed the Impugned
APR Order dated 31.03.2025 for FY 2021-22.
14. Aggrieved by the Impugned Order dated 31.03.2025, the Appellants have
preferred the present Appeal.
15. The Appellants have prayed for the following relief before us:
“a) set aside the Annual Performance Review/ Tariff order dated
31.3.2025, passed by the Ld. West Bengal Electricity Regulatory
Commission in Case No. APR-125/ 24-25 to the extent challenged in
the present appeal;
b) pass such other order(s), as this Hon’ble Tribunal may deem fit and
proper in the facts and circumstances of the case.”
16. The appeal had challenged Impugned Order on several issues. However, as
recorded in the daily order dated 12th May 2026 for the Appeal No. 15 of 2026 &
IA No. 1074 of 2025, Learned Counsels for Appellant as well as Respondents,
submitted that, the submissions which have been made on the issue of interest on
differential AFC during the course of hearing on the interim application are similar
which would be made at the time of final disposal of the appeal on this issue.
Therefore, at the request of the Learned Counsels, we are taking up this appeal
for final disposal on this issue. Accordingly, in this judgement we are only dealing
with the issue of interest on differential AFC. So far as remaining issues are
Page 9 of 41

Judgement in Appeal No. 15 of 2026
concerned, the Appellants are given liberty to agitate those issues by way of fresh
appeal.
Issues for Consideration
17. Based on the submissions of the Appellants, we have identified following
issues for our consideration:
1. Whether the original APR Order had attained finality and could not be
reopened.
2. Whether the introduction of the empirical formula after the original APR
Order had attained finality is legally permissible.
3. Whether the empirical formula results in an artificial reduction of the
principal differential Annual Fixed Charges (AFC).
4. Whether the impugned order suffers from lack of reasoning.
5. Whether the impugned approach results in dual treatment leading to
consumer prejudice.
6. Whether the review petitions were beyond the jurisdiction of the State
Commission.
7. Whether Regulation 2.5.3 supports the adoption of the empirical
formula.
Submissions of the Parties, Our Analysis and Conclusion
“I think that it is a relatively good approximation to
truth—which is much too complicated to allow
anything but approximations—that mathematical
ideas originate in empirics.”
Page 10 of 41

Judgement in Appeal No. 15 of 2026
— John von Neumann
(one of the most influential mathematicians of the twentieth
century)
18. The present case revolves around what has been described as an “empirical
formula”. Empirical methods and formulas have played, and continue to play, an
important role in science, engineering, economics and several other fields. As the
observation of John von Neumann suggests, the distinction between empirical
observation and mathematical formulation is often less rigid than it may first
appear.
19. In the present matter, however, the principal question is not whether the
formula under consideration can properly be characterised as empirical. Rather,
the more fundamental issue is whether the adoption and application of the formula
was justified in the facts and circumstances of the case. The question as to the
nature of the formula itself, including whether it is truly empirical or is founded upon
identifiable technical and engineering principles, shall be examined in the
succeeding part of this judgement.
Issue 1: Whether the original APR Order had attained finality and
could not be reopened.
Submissions of the Appellants
20. The Appellants submitted that the retail tariff order dated 25.05.2015 had
adopted CERC approved AFC for FY 2013-14 as the input cost for FY 2014-15 to
FY 2016-17, subject to truing-up. In the APR Petition for FY 2014-17, DVC itself
claimed interest on differential AFC under Regulation 8(13) of the CERC Tariff
Page 11 of 41

Judgement in Appeal No. 15 of 2026
Regulations, 2014, linking AFC recovery to availability of stations and the T&D
network under Regulation 30.
21. The Appellants contended that the APR Order dated 08.06.2023 accepted
DVC’s claim, computed differential AFC as the difference between tariff-order AFC
and trued-up AFC and allowed interest thereon for specified stations and the T&D
system. A revenue gap of Rs. 175.66 Crore was determined and later recovered
through the ARR Order dated 13.03.2024.
22. However, DVC never challenged this methodology and the computation of
interest on differential AFC had attained finality. It could not have been reopened
in subsequent proceedings.
Submissions of WBERC
23. For the first time in FY 2014-17 APR proceedings, DVC claimed interest
under Regulation 8(13) of the CERC Tariff Regulations, which WBERC allowed
vide Order dated 08.06.2023. However, WBERC denied that the issue had
attained finality. The said order was conditional and kept open for final
quantification pending CERC true-up orders for several stations including BTPS
‘B’, CTPS U# 1-3, DTPS U# 3 & 4, MTPS U# 7 & 8 and others. Reliance was
placed on paragraphs 4.5.3 and 5.5 of the Order dated 08.06.2023, where DVC
was directed to compute adjustment amounts based on subsequent true-up orders
and submit the same in subsequent APR proceedings.
24. The impugned order merely implemented those directions; therefore, the
principles of res judicata or finality were inapplicable. The computation was not in
the nature of review but was a compliance exercise. Since fixed cost itself was
Page 12 of 41

Judgement in Appeal No. 15 of 2026
subject to future adjustment, the consequential interest component also
necessarily remained open for final determination.
Submissions of DVC
25. DVC submitted that the Appellants’ contention that the APR Order dated
08.06.2023 conclusively determined the issue was untenable. The Order dated
31.03.2025 was neither a reopening nor a new methodology, but a continuation
and rectification of a pending computational exercise necessitated by availability
of complete CERC true-up data and alignment of projected-sales-based AFC with
actual-sales-based AFC.
26. The APR Order dated 08.06.2023 expressly kept the issue open. Reliance
was placed on paragraph 4.5.3, where WBERC recorded that trued-up AFC for
several stations had not been determined by CERC and directed DVC to furnish
revised computations upon issuance of CERC true-up orders. The figure of Rs.
51.82 Crore was provisional and based on incomplete data. After final CERC true-
up orders, DVC submitted reconciled computations considered by WBERC in the
APR Order dated 31.03.2025, resulting in revised determination of Rs. 252.19
Crore.
27. The exercise did not alter the methodology of tariff determination but merely
corrected a mathematical inconsistency arising from comparison of AFC figures
computed on different sales bases.

Analysis and Conclusion
28. Both WBERC and DVC have relied on paragraph 4.5.3 and 5.5 of the
WBERC APR Order dated 08.06.2023. The relevant extracts of the aforesaid
paragraphs are reproduced below:
“4.5.3 DVC in the instant petition had submitted the available Truing-up Orders of
CERC leading to determination of the Fixed Cost of the transmission tariff for
integrated transmission and distribution (T&D) system of DVC dated 02.03.2022 and
10.06.2022 for new and existing elements respectively. Further, they submitted that
trueing up orders for power stations of DVC were yet to be issued by the Central
Commission at the time of submission of the petition dated 14.07.2022 and prayed
for considering issuance of APR orders based on their submission. However, the
Commission has observed from the website of CERC that till 31.03.2023, trueing up
orders have been issued by CERC for MTPS U#1-3, MTPS U#4, MTPS U#5&6,
MHS, THS, PHS and third order of integrated T&D system of DVC for the period
2014 - 15 to 2018 - 19. The Commission finds it prudent to consider the input cost
as per the True up orders for the period 2014 - 15 to 2018 - 19 issued by CERC upto
31.03.2023 for finalization of APR for the years 2014 - 15, 2015 - 16 and 2016 - 17.
In respect of the other power stations of DVC for which trueing up order has not been
issued by CERC till 31.03.2023, fixed costs as per MYT orders are considered.
Therefore, the Commission considers Truing-up Orders in respect of MTPS U#1-3,
MTPS U#4, MTPS U#5&6, MHS, THS and PHS in determination of proportionate

the period 2014 - 15 to 2018 - 19 in respect of integrated T&D system of DVC have
been considered for allocation of fixed cost of T&D system. The list of orders of
CERC considered by the Commission are as tabulated below:

29. It is evident that the issue relating to the cumulative AFC of all generating
stations, and the transmission & distribution system had not attained finality.
WBERC had kept the matter open because the true-up orders for certain
generating stations had not been issued by CERC at that stage. While nothing has
Page 15 of 41

been brought to our notice that WBERC specifically contemplated an adjustment
on account of difference between projected and actual energy sales, the fact
remains that the determination itself had not reached finality. Under these
circumstances, we find no infirmity in carrying out any other adjustment that is
otherwise justified and necessary while arriving at the final value. Whether the
adjustment carried out in the Impugned Order on account of the impact of variation
between projected and actual energy sales on AFC recovery was justified or not
shall be analysed by us in the subsequent part of this judgement.
Issue 2: Whether the introduction of the empirical formula after
the original APR Order had attained finality is legally permissible.
Submissions of the Appellants
30. The Appellants contended that only after realizing that trued-up AFC was
substantially lower than the tariff-order AFC did DVC devise a new “empirical
formula”. This formula was never pleaded in the original APR proceedings but was
introduced subsequently through review petitions and later through Annexure-3 to
the APR Petition for FY 2021-22.
31. The Impugned APR Order dated 31.03.2025 adopted this formula by
artificially reducing the tariff-order AFC in proportion to actual sales against
projected sales, thereby reducing or eliminating the differential AFC for interest
computation.
Submissions of the WBERC
32. WBERC contended that regulatory consistency required the same corrected
methodology to be uniformly applied across all generating stations within the same
Page 16 of 41

control period. It would have been arbitrary to apply one methodology to previously
trued-up stations and another to subsequently trued-up stations.
33. WBERC further contended that the impugned computation was not in the
nature of review but was a compliance exercise undertaken pursuant to the liberty
granted in the earlier order. Since fixed cost itself was subject to future adjustment
upon issuance of pending CERC true-up orders, the consequential interest
component also necessarily remained open for final determination.
Submissions of DVC
34. DVC denied introduction of any new “empirical formula”. WBERC merely
finalized the pending computation for FY 2014-17 after issuance of CERC true-up
orders by applying the same approach already adopted in Review APR Orders
dated 24.03.2025 for FY 2017-18, FY 2018-19 and FY 2019-20.
35. DVC noted that Appellants challenged the methodology only for FY 2014-17
and FY 2019-20 where it resulted in amounts receivable by consumers, but
consciously refrained from challenging it for FY 2017-18 and FY 2018-19 where it
substantially reduced DVC’s interest liability from Rs. 317.76 Crore to Rs. 155.59
Crore and from Rs. 69.47 Crore to Rs. 16.59 Crore respectively.
36. According to DVC, Appellants could not approbate and reprobate. Reliance
was placed on Talwandi Sabo Power Limited vs. Punjab State Electricity
Regulatory Commission, Appeal No. 21 of 2019 and State of Punjab vs. Dhanjit
Singh Sandhu, (2014) 15 SCC 144.

Judgement in Appeal No. 15 of 2026
Analysis and Conclusion
37. We have already concluded under Issue 1 that the AFC order had not
attained finality. In regard to contention of DVC that the Appellants have covered
these issues in the appeals selectively only for the years when revised AFC had
reduced from original AFC, during the hearing, Ld. Counsel for the Appellants Mr.
Rajiv Yadav had clarified that in-principle they do not agree with the methodology
of truing up based on empirical formula for all the years, but had no ground to
object to it in the years in which they had gained financially due to such adjustment
as they were not adversely affected. We are satisfied with this explanation. It is
clear that the application of the “Empirical formula” has benefitted consumers in
some years and to the DVC in other years, and therefore, the apprehension of
DVPCA is unfounded that this formula was devised after realizing that the trued-
up AFC was lower than the AFC considered in the original tariff order. Whatever
conclusion we arrive at in this Appeal, may get applied consistently in all those
years where the relevant orders have been challenged before us in the form of
Appeals.
Issue 3: Whether the empirical formula results in an artificial
reduction of the principal differential Annual Fixed Charges
(AFC).
Submissions of the Appellants
38. The Appellants submitted that by way of an illustration, if tariff-order AFC was
Rs. 100 and trued-up AFC was Rs. 80, the differential AFC ought to remain Rs.
20, on which interest should be payable. Under the empirical formula, the tariff-
order AFC is first scaled down by the ratio of actual sales to projected sales, so
that the differential becomes zero.

deprives consumers of the interest otherwise due.

Submissions of the WBERC
40. WBERC submitted that the earlier methodology resulted in an “Apples to
Oranges” comparison by contrasting projected AFC values with actual trued-up
costs without accounting for actual sales. The previous approach effectively

95. Appellants’ contention that differential AFC along with interest already stood
adjusted through revenue gap determined in APR Order dated 08.06.2023 for FY
2014-17 was factually incorrect. Subsequent Tariff Order dated 31.03.2025
demonstrated revenue gap arising from prior periods had not been fully adjusted
at one instance but carried forward and adjusted in phased manner across multiple
tariff periods.
96. State Commission recorded only part of total regulatory assets/ revenue gap
which had been adjusted in earlier years including FY 2023-24 and FY 2024-25

while balance amount carried forward for adjustment in FY 2025-26 and
subsequent years. Appellants’ premise that entire revenue gap stood finally
recovered pursuant to Order dated 08.06.2023 was untenable since regulatory
framework contemplated staggered recovery over multiple control periods.
97. Determination and adjustment of revenue gap is ongoing regulatory exercise
wherein under-recovery or over-recovery is trued up and adjusted across
successive tariff orders. Adjustment of revenue gap arising from differential AFC
was merely consequential outcome of underlying cost determination.
98. In any event, rectification is independently traceable to Regulation 2.5.3(v)
of WBERC Tariff Regulations, 2011 which expressly permits correction of any
miscalculation in ensuing Tariff Order or Annual Performance Review; correction

substituting an incorrect value with the correct one, others may require a
computational methodology to quantify the necessary correction.
100. The omission in the earlier orders was the failure to account for the impact
of variation between projected and actual energy sales on AFC recovery. The

1. This Appeal is filed by Power Transmission Corporation of Uttarakhand
Limited (“PTCUL”/ “Appellant”) challenging the Impugned Order dated 31.03.2021
passed by the Central Electricity Regulatory Commission (“CERC”/ “Respondent
No. 2”) in Petition No. 104/TT/2020.
Page 4 of 46

Judgement in Appeal No. 410 of 2022
Description of the Parties
2. The Appellant, PTCUL is a company incorporated under the Companies Act,
1956 and discharges the functions of a State Transmission Utility (STU) in the
State of Uttarakhand under Section 2(67) read with Section 39 of the Electricity
Act, 2003 (“Act”).
3. The Respondent No.1, Power Grid Corporation of India Limited (“PGCIL”),
the original Petitioner in Petition No.104/TT/2020, is a deemed transmission
licsensee under the Act.
4. The Respondent No. 2, the Central Electricity Regulatory Commission
(CERC), is a statutory regulatory body constituted under Section 76 of the
Electricity Act, 2003.
5. The Respondent Nos. 3 to 19, are distribution licensees/ utilities/ state
administration departments in terms of the Act.
Factual Matrix of the Case
6. The present Appeal arises out of the Order dated 31.03.2021 (“Impugned
Order”) passed by the CERC whereby the Commercial Operation Date (COD) of
certain transmission assets (Asset-III) was approved and consequential liability
towards transmission charges was fastened upon the Appellant.
7. In the 23rd Standing Committee Meeting (SCM) held on 16.02.2008 at
Dehradun, the scheme for construction of a 400/220 kV substation at Dehradun
by Respondent No. 1 was inter-alia discussed and standard norms regarding the
number of bays for substations were adopted. According to these agreed norms,
six 220 kV line bays were planned at Dehradun. Out of these, on 01.02.2017, two
Page 5 of 46

Judgement in Appeal No. 410 of 2022
bays were utilized by the Appellant for actuating the 220 kV D/c Jhajra-Sherpur1
line. Thereafter, on 04.02.2017, all six 220 kV line bays were decalred under
commercial operation by Respondent No. 1; however, four bays remained
unutilized due to the non-commissioning of the downstream network.
8. The Appellant-PTCUL was requested to inform utilization plan for these bays
at various points of time. Finally, the Respondent No. 1-PGCIL, by letter dated
20.03.2017, informed the Appellant about the commissioning of the transmission
system and highlighted that four bays remained unutilized, requesting a utilization
plan. The Appellant, however, only undertook internal correspondence dated
30.06.2017 and 27.12.2017 exploring possible future utilization of these bays
which were not communicated to Respondent No. 1.
9. In Petition No. 55/TT/2017, CERC passed an order dated 30.11.2017
determining COD and tariff for Asset-I but declined to approve COD and tariff for
the remaining four bays (termed Asset-II at that point of time but were temed Asset-
III in the Impugned Order), observing that the said assets were not put to regular
service due to the absence of downstream connectivity. Respondent No. 1’s
Review Petition No. 8/RP/2018 against the said order was dismissed by CERC on
12.06.2018.
10. Meanwhile, on 20.12.2018, Long Term Access (LTA) was granted to M/s
SJVN for the Naitwar Mori HEP, requiring implementation of a 220 kV D/c Mori-
Dehradun line along with bays at the Dehradun substation. A Tripartite Agreement
1 It is noted that that while PGCIL calls the sub-station as Dehradun sub-station, PTCUL names
it as Sherpur sub-station. Sherpur is a village and locality within the Dehradun district of
Uttarakhand.
Page 6 of 46

dated 31.01.2020 was executed between the Appellant, Respondent No. 1 and
M/s SJVN in this regard.
11. Thereafter, Respondent No. 1 filed Petition No. 104/TT/2020 before CERC
on 06.01.2020 seeking truing-up of tariff and approval of COD for the four
unutilized bays (now termed as Asset-III) as 04.02.2017. During the proceedings,
the Appellant was impleaded as a party for the first time on 25.02.2020.
12. Meanwhile, the issue of implementation of the Mori-Dehradun line was
discussed in the 3rd meeting of NRPC Transmission Planning held on 19.02.2021,
wherein it was agreed that the line may be implemented under the Central Sector.
13. By the Impugned Order dated 31.03.2021, CERC approved the COD of
Asset-III as 04.02.2017 and held the Appellant liable to bear transmission charges
from the said date till the commissioning of the downstream network.
14. Pursuant to the Impugned Order, Respondent No. 1 raised monthly bilateral
bills upon the Appellant towards transmission charges for Asset-III from November
2021 onwards.
15. The Appellant challenged the Impugned Order by filing a Review Petition No.
21/RP/2021 before CERC; however, the same was dismissed by order dated
27.05.2022. During this period, the issue regarding utilization of the four bays was
also discussed in the 50th meeting of the Northern Regional Power Committee held
on 28.01.2022, wherein no decision was taken in view of the pendency of the
matter before CERC.

16. Aggrieved by the Impugned Order dated 31.03.2021 and the subsequent
dismissal of the review petition, the Appellant has preferred the present Appeal.
17. The Appellant has prayed for the following relief before us:
“A. allow the present appeal and set-aside the Impugned Order
dated 31.03.2021 passed by the Ld. Central Electricity
Regulatory Commission in Petition No. 104/TT/2020 to the
extent that it has determined the COD for Asset-III as 04.02.2017
under proviso (ii) of Regulation 4(3) of the 2014 Tariff
Regulations, and has held the Appellant to be liable to build the
downstream networks and liable to bear the yearly transmission
charges for Asset-Ill from COD on 04.02.2017 to COD of the
downstream networks;
B. declare and hold that PTCUL/Appellant is/was not liable to
make the downstream asset with respect to Asset-Ill;
C. declare and hold that PTCUL/Appellant is not liable to pay
yearly transmission charges of the Asset-Ill;
D. quash and set aside the bills (refer para 7.34) raised by the
Respondent No.1 upon the Appellant seeking payment of
transmission charges for Asset-Ill; and
E Pass such further or other orders as may be deemed
necessary in the facts and circumstances of the present appeal.”
Page 8 of 46

Issues for Consideration
18. After hearing the Learned Senior Counsel for the Appellant and the Learned
Counsel for the Respondent at length and carefully considering their respective
submissions, we have also examined the written pleadings and relevant material
on record. We have framed the following issues for our consideration mainly based
on the submissions of the Appellant:
Issue 1: Whether the minutes of meetings and related correspondence, in
the absence of any Contractual or statutory provision create any binding
obligation on PTCUL to construct downstream assets?
Issue 2: Can PTCUL be made to pay transmission charges for the subject
bays, particularly under the PoC-based regime applicable during 2014-2019.
Issue 3: Can COD of the subject bays be declared without actual utilization?
Issue 4: Whether the Impugned Order is vitiated by deviation from CERC’s
earlier orders on the same asset?
Issue 5: Do record establish that the bays were constructed for PTCUL?
Issue 6: Whether PGCIL’s own conduct, including delay in commissioning
the bays, non-impleadment of PTCUL in initial tariff proceedings and later
tripartite LTA arrangements, operates as estoppel against any allegation of
prior binding obligation on PTCUL?
Page 9 of 46

Judgement in Appeal No. 410 of 2022
Submissions of the Parties, Our Analysis and Conclusions
Issue 1: Whether the minutes of meetings and related
correspondence, in the absence of any Contractual or statutory
provision create any binding obligation on PTCUL to construct
downstream assets?
Submissions of PTCUL
19. The Appellant submits that CERC and PGCIL have proceeded on an
erroneous legal premise in treating minutes of a planning forum as
constituting consensus ad idem so as to create binding financial liability upon
PTCUL. It is contended that consensus ad idem requires a concluded and
enforceable agreement with clear intention to create legal relations, certainty of
terms and enforceability, which is admittedly absent in the present case.
20. It is contended that the minutes of Standing Committee meetings (SCMs)
and NRPC meetings are characterised as mere coordination and planning
documents, which do not, by themselves, constitute contracts or impose
obligations in the absence of any implementation agreement, TSA, LTA or other
binding instrument. The Appellant submits that its participation in such statutory
planning meetings and routine system-planning correspondence was in discharge
of its statutory functions as State Transmission Utility and cannot be retrospectively
construed as creating commercial liability or enforceable obligations.
21. It is specifically denied by PTCUL that the 23rd SCM reflects any agreement
that the six 220 kV bays were constructed for PTCUL or that PTCUL assumed any
obligation to develop downstream connectivity or to bear any transmission charges
for the subject bays. The minutes do not record any agreement, commitment or
Page 10 of 46

Judgement in Appeal No. 410 of 2022
allocation of tariff liability upon PTCUL, nor do they stipulate any timelines for
downstream implementation that could be enforced as contractual obligations.
Submissions of PGCIL
22. PGCIL disputes PTCUL’s plea of absence of consensus ad idem and
contends that consensus within the statutory transmission-planning framework is
established through deliberations and recorded decisions in SCM and NRPC
meetings. According to PGCIL, the 23rd SCM dated 16.02.2008, read with the 25th
SCM dated 17.07.2008, records agreement of all stakeholders, including PTCUL,
that six 220 kV line bays at Dehradun substation would be constructed by PGCIL
for PTCUL’s use.
23. PGCIL further relies on subsequent SCMs (34th on 08.08.2014, 36th on
13.07.2015, 37th on 20.01.2016 and 38th on 30.05.2016) to submit that the
understanding regarding matching development of upstream and downstream
systems was repeatedly reiterated and that PTCUL indicated that its 220 kV
system from Dehradun would be ready by March 2015. In the 41st NRPC meeting
dated 27.02.2018, PTCUL itself is stated to have proposed specific utilization of
the bays for Dehradun-Naugaon and Dehradun-Selaqui lines, and in the 42nd
NRPC meeting dated 28.06.2018 to have provided a concrete utilization plan
including Yamuna basin projects.
24. PGCIL also relies on its letters issued between 2013 and 2017 seeking
updates on downstream connectivity, which were received without objection, and
on internal correspondence of PTCUL (including letters dated 30.06.2017 and
27.12.2017) acknowledging planned utilization of the six bays. On this basis,
PGCIL submits that there was a clear and continuing meeting of minds and that
Page 11 of 46

Judgement in Appeal No. 410 of 2022
formal execution of a TSA/LTA was not a pre-condition for PTCUL’s obligations to
arise in this statutory planning context.
Analysis & Conclusions
25. It is settled position of law that even an oral agreement can be construed as
contract, if such oral agreement encompasses a concluded agreement on all
material terms and the parties intended to be bound at that stage, then the contract
is complete even though a later formal document is contemplated. (Kollipara
Sriramulu v. T. Aswathanarayana, 1968 SCC OnLine SC 87).
26. It must be kept in mind that in India, electricity sector is governed by policies,
rules and regulations issued under the Act. Further, the transmission segment of
electricity sector is closely regulated. Therefore, it is essential that we first look at
the policy prescription in the National Electricity Policy (NEP) issued in February,
2005. The relevant part of paragraph 5.3.2 of the NEP is reproduced below:
“5.3.2 Keeping in view the massive increase planned in generation and also for
development of power market, there is need for adequately augmenting transmission
capacity. While planning new generation capacities, requirement of associated
transmission capacity would need to be worked out simultaneously in order to avoid
mismatch between generation capacity and transmission facilities. The policy
emphasizes the following to meet the above objective:
……
•
……..
•
• Network expansion should be planned and implemented keeping in view the
anticipated transmission needs that would be incident on the system in the open
access regime. Prior agreement with the beneficiaries would not be a pre-
condition for network expansion. CTU/STU should undertake network
expansion after identifying the requirements in consultation with stakeholders
and taking up the execution after due regulatory approvals.
•
……”
(Emphasis Supplied)
Page 12 of 46

Judgement in Appeal No. 410 of 2022
27. Further, Section 3.4 (b) of the Indian Electricity Grid Code issued by CERC
in 2006 (IEGC 2006), provides as under:
“3.4 Planning Policy
(a)…
….
(c) In addition to the major inter-State transmission system, the CTU shall plan, from
time to time, system strengthening schemes, need of which may arise to overcome
the constraints in power transfer and to improve the overall performance of the grid.
The inter-State transmission proposals including system strengthening
scheme identified on the basis of the planning studies would be discussed,
reviewed and finalized in the meetings of Regional Standing Committees for
Transmission Planning constituted by CEA, in consultation with the
beneficiaries, RPC, CEA and the RLDC.
…..”
(Emphasis Supplied)
28. The revised IEGC was issued by CERC in 2010 and the relevant provision
reads as under:
“3.4 Planning Philosophy
(a)…
….
(c) In addition to the inter-State transmission system, the CTU shall plan, from time
to time, system strengthening schemes, need of which may arise to overcome the
constraints in power transfer and to improve the overall performance of the grid. The
inter-state transmission proposals including system strengthening scheme
identified on the basis of the planning studies would be discussed, reviewed
and finalized in the meetings of Regional Standing Committees for
Transmission Planning constituted by CEA, in consultation with the Regional
Entities, RPC, CEA, NLDC and the RLDC and action may be taken by CTU on
the basis of Power Purchase Agreements (PPAs) signed with the beneficiaries.
In case of associated transmission system where all PPAs have not yet been signed,
and where agreement could not be reached in respect of system strengthening
schemes, the CTU may approach CERC for the regulatory approval in accordance
with Central Electricity Regulatory Commission (Grant of Regulatory Approval for
Capital Investment to CTU for execution of Inter-State Transmission Scheme)
Regulations, as and when they come into force .
…….”
(Emphasis Supplied)
Page 13 of 46

Judgement in Appeal No. 410 of 2022
29. A combined reading of the relevant policy prescriptions and the provisions of
the IEGC demonstrates that the process of transmission system planning
undertaken in the meetings of the Regional Standing Committee (referred to as
“SCM” in the present case) has the requisite regulatory sanction. Further, it is well
recognised that certain terms and conditions that would ordinarily form part of a
contract, including the determination and recovery of transmission charges,
emanate from and are governed by the applicable Regulations. Therefore, in our
considered view, the Minutes of Meeting may constitute a contractual framework,
provided that the essential terms are sufficiently crystallised, including, inter alia,
the identity of the entity responsible for development of the transmission system
(either on its own or through another agency) and the timelines for execution of
such works. If there is no agreement on necessity of a transmission element, then
also in line with NEP, the agencies responsible for planning namely CEA and CTU
can decide to go ahead, if they are convinced about requirement of such element.
However, in line with the settled position of law, we are of the opinion that the
implementing agency and time lines must be recorded in the minutes of the
meeting (“MOM”) to construe it as contract, both for ISTS element as well as
downstream intra-state element(s) essential for utilisation of the ISTS element.
30. In this context, we intend to examine all the MOM and correspondence relied
upon by the PGCIL to contend that PTCUL had agreed to utilize all the six 220 kV
bays at Dehradun:
(a) 23rd SCM meeting held on 16.02.2008
31. The first and perhaps most important document is the minutes of 23rd SCM
held on 16.02.2008. The relevant part of the MOM is extracted below:
Page 14 of 46

Judgement in Appeal No. 410 of 2022
“6.0 Region System Strengthening Scheme - New Proposal
6.1 It was also discussed and agreed that in view of increasing demand density
the norm of providing 220 kV bays with 400/220 kV transformers would be revised
as following:-
• For 2x315 MVA - 6 nos. of line bays
• For 3rd 315 MVA transformer - 2 line bays
• For 500 MVA transformer - 4 nos. of line bays
6.2 It was discussed and agreed that for meeting the increasing demands
and increasing quantum of power supply required to be delivered from
regional grid to state grids, there was need for providing new regional grid
400kV substations at Manesar in Haryana, Kotputli and Neemrana in Rajasthan,
Hapur and Bagpat in U.P, Hamirpur in H.P, Dehradun in Uttrakhand (this would
also facilitate power evacuation from Kotlibhel HEP), New Wanpoh and one s/s for
Jammu in J&K and S/S capacity augmentation at Patiala and Malerkotla in Punjab.
Of these, s/s at Manesar and Bagpat would be GIS and s/s at Neemrana, Hapur,
Hamirpur, Dehradun and other places could be GIS or open yard depending on
availability of space.”
(Emphasis supplied)
32. It emerges that the broad consensus amongst the participants (and not just
PGCIL and PTCUL), inter-alia was that from then onwards, whenever a sub-station
with 2 x 315 MVA 400/220 kV transformers would get established, there will be six
number of bays on 220 kV side. The provision of six 220 kV bays appears to be in
consonance with the planning requirement for adequate downstream evacuation
arrangement, while maintaining the requisite redundancy and operational
flexibility. Each 220 kV bay can typically facilitate transfer of the order of 200-300
MW of power, though the actual capability would depend upon the characteristics,
configuration and rating of the downstream 220 kV transmission line. Though the
Page 15 of 46

Judgement in Appeal No. 410 of 2022
Dehradun Sub-station was intended to cater to the anticipated increase in demand
in Uttarakhand, there is nothing on record to indicate the extent of demand growth
that was envisaged to be served through the said Sub-station in the ensuing years.
In the absence of such material, we are inclined to conclude that the six bays were
created in accordance with the agreed planning norms and were not intended
exclusively for power drawal by Uttarakhand. Also, there is no mention of the date
by which these bays were to be ready, which in our view, is one of the essential
conditions for MOM to be construed as contract.
(b) 34th SCM meeting held on 08.08.2014
33. Next, reliance is placed by the PGCIL on the minutes of the 34th SCM
meeting. In this meeting, under the item “Establishment of new 400/220 kV
substations in NR”, the statement of GM, PTCUL is recorded as under:
“GM, PTCUL stated that their 220 kV system for 400 kV Dehradun would be
available by March 2015 matching with the commissioning of the substation”
34. PGCIL has contended, and the CERC has concluded, that PTCUL, during
the said meeting, had assured completion of the downstream assets
corresponding to all six bays by March 2015. However, PTCUL has submitted that
their representative was only speaking about Sherpur (PGCIL)- Jhajra line. In our
opinion, the expression “their 220 kV system” merely denotes the 220 kV
transmission lines being developed by PTCUL and cannot, by itself, be read as a
commitment to utilise all six 220 kV bays envisaged at the Sub-station. The record
is devoid of any indication as to the number of bays that were intended to be
utilised for those lines. Further, now, it is clear (from the internal correspondence
of PTCUL dated 30.06.2017 and 27.12.2017 relied upon by PGCIL) that in the
worst case scenario against PTCUL, it can be said that it was contemplating
constructing downstream transmission lines for use of all the bays, but the
Page 16 of 46

Judgement in Appeal No. 410 of 2022
execution of transmission lines connecting to remaining four bays had not started.
In such a scenario, it is unlikely that GM, PTCUL in a meeting held in August 2014
could have promised completion of entire downstream network using all six 220
kV bays within 8 months so as to be ready by March 2015. It is surprising that none
of the participants in the meeting, including PGCIL requested PTCUL to furnish
details of the downstream network being constructed, which would have brought
clarity that seems to be missing in the hindsight.
(c) 36th SCM meeting held on 13.07.2015
35. We find that the only relevant part recorded in this MOM in the relevant
context is as under:
“25. Establishment of new 400/220kV substations in Northern Region:

(d) 37th SCM meeting held on 20.01.2016
37. The discussions in the 37th SCM meeting on the relevant issue proceeded

“29.0 Establishment of new 400/220kV substations in Northern Region:

Totala v. Hemant Vithal Kamat & Ors., (2021) 9 SCC 99, and DSR Steel (Pvt.) Ltd.
v. State of Rajasthan & Ors., (2012) 6 SCC 782, an order rejecting review is not
appealable and does not itself create rights. PGCIL also points out that CERC is
empowered under Regulation 4(3) of the 2014 Tariff Regulations to approve COD
Page 35 of 46

Judgement in Appeal No. 410 of 2022
and determine liability for mismatch periods and that this position has been
affirmed by the Hon’ble Supreme Court in Power Grid Corporation of India Ltd. v.
Madhya Pradesh Power Transmission Co. Ltd., 2025 SCC OnLine SC 1128.
81. On this basis, PGCIL contends that the Impugned Order is not a deviation
from a concluded earlier view attracting issue estoppel, but a substantive
determination made in the exercise of regulatory powers upon satisfaction of
conditions for COD under the second proviso.
Analysis and Conclusions
82. The relevant paragraph 23 of the CERC order dated 30.11.2017 is extracted
below:
“23. It is observed that Asset-II is not in regular service due to non-availability of
associated downstream transmission system under the scope of PTCUL and
therefore, the COD of Asset-II is not considered in the instant order. The petitioner
is directed to file fresh petition matching with the associated downstream
transmission system.”
83. PGCIL had filed a review petition No. 8/RP/2018 inter-alia on the issue of not
approving deemed commercial operation of the asset. The CERC vide order dated
12.06.2018 rejected the prayer for review expressing that the contention of PGCIL
falls in the scope of appeal and not review. However, PGCIL made a fresh request
for allowing COD of unused 4 Nos. of bays at Dehradun in the Petition No.
104/TT/2020, which was primarily filed for truing up of transmission tariff for some
already commissioned assets relatable to Dehradun sub-station. This time CERC
agreed to the request and allowed COD of these bays with effect from 04.02.2017
under proviso (ii) of Regulation 4.3 of the Tariff Regulations 2014.
Page 36 of 46

Judgement in Appeal No. 410 of 2022
84. We do not find merit in contention of PTCUL that CERC’s earlier orders
dated 30.11.2017 (Petition No. 55/TT/2017) and 12.06.2018 (Petition No.
8/RP/2018) had attained finality; and that CERC has erred in allowing COD having
rejected the same in earlier order. We agree with the contention of PGCIL that the
CERC had merely deferred consideration of the issue and intended to examine it
upon the development of the downstream network. Whether such deferment was
justified is a separate question, and does not fall for consideration in the present
appeal. Since the CERC had not taken any final view, the argument of PTCUL,
that CERC should have given detailed reasons for deviating from earlier position,
also collapses.
85. At the same time, we are of the view that consideration of the issue could
not have been deferred indefinitely. To hold otherwise would lead to anomalous
consequences. For instance, if the downstream network were not to be
commissioned during the entire economic life of the bays, the issue would remain
unresolved indefinitely. Nothing in Regulation 4(3) of the Tariff Regulations, 2014
mandates that a determination regarding COD under proviso (ii) can be made only
upon actual utilisation of the asset. The regulation does not preclude the CERC
from taking a decision on the basis of the facts and circumstances available at the
relevant point in time.
86. In view of the forgoing analysis, we find no error in the CERC allowing the
COD of the asset. The earlier orders cannot be construed as having conclusively
determined the issue; they merely deferred its consideration pending the
occurrence of relevant events. Consequently, the CERC was not precluded from
examining and deciding the issue in the Impugned Order.

Judgement in Appeal No. 410 of 2022
Issue 5: Do record establish that the bays were constructed for
PTCUL?
Submissions of PTCUL
87. The Appellant has contended that the subject 220 kV bays at the 400/220
kV Sherpur, Dehradun substation were conceived and implemented by PGCIL in
accordance with standard inter-State transmission planning norms as part of the
Northern Region System Strengthening Scheme (NRSS-XVIII), and not pursuant
to any specific request or requirement of PTCUL. As per the minutes of the 23rd
SCM, the six 220 kV bays at the 400 kV substation were not exclusively planned
for PTCUL or for meeting State demand; two bays were envisaged for evacuation
of power from NHPC’s Kotlibhel HEP, while PTCUL had only internally explored
utilization of two bays for the proposed 220 kV double-circuit Mori-Dehradun line,
which plan was never finalized or implemented.
88. It is submitted that Kotlibhel HEP did not materialise, and that the Mori-
Dehradun proposal later evolved into an arrangement under which responsibilities
were allocated to PTCUL pursuant to LTA intimation dated 20.12.2018 and
tripartite LTA agreement dated 31.01.2020, which was itself revisited in the 3rd
NRPC (Transmission Planning) meeting on 19.02.2021 contemplating Central
Sector implementation subject to materialisation of generation projects in the
Yamuna basin. Under these circumstances, the Appellant contends that the
subject bays were planned as part of a broader regional and
generation-evacuation framework, and that their cost ought to be borne by regional
beneficiaries through the PoC mechanism rather than being exclusively saddled
on PTCUL.
89. It is further submitted that ISTS assets developed under
system-strengthening schemes are intended to serve the entire grid, and that

under the 2010 Sharing Regulations, as clarified by the Second Amendment to the
Sharing Regulations, 2020, recovery of such charges is to be through pooled or
component-based allocation, including from the relevant Drawee DIC (UPCL),
rather than through unilateral billing upon PTCUL. The Appellant points out that
PGCIL’s own subsequent conduct in ceasing billing upon PTCUL from December
2023 and seeking recovery through the PoC pool is consistent with this position
and undermines any claim that the bays were always meant to be exclusively
chargeable to PTCUL.
Submissions of PGCIL
90. PGCIL submits that Asset-III (the subject bays), conceptualised and
approved as part of NRSS-XVIII in the 23rd SCM, is distinct and independent from
the transmission network associated with the 60 MW Naitwar Mori HEP, which was
planned much later. LTA intimation for Naitwar Mori was issued only on
20.12.2018, nearly a decade after planning of Asset-III, demonstrating, according
to PGCIL, that the scheme associated with Naitwar Mori and the tripartite LTA
agreement with PTCUL and SJVN are unrelated to the subject bays that form part
of NRSS-XVIII.
91. PGCIL therefore contends that it was not required to furnish LTA-related
details in the tariff proceedings for Asset-III, which were confined to determination
of tariff for NRSS-XVIII assets and not governed by the subsequent LTA
arrangement for Naitwar Mori. As regards cost allocation under the later regime,
PGCIL points out that, pursuant to the Second Amendment to the Sharing
Regulations, 2020, the subject assets have been classified under the “Transformer
Component” for Uttarakhand, with transmission charges payable by UPCL from
01.11.2023.

92. Without prejudice, PGCIL submits that for the prior mismatch period, even if
COD were notionally aligned with downstream readiness for PoC purposes, IDC
and IEDC for the intervening period would require capitalization to ensure
legitimate cost recovery through tariff from November 2023 onwards. PGCIL thus
maintains that the Impugned Order’s allocation of liability on PTCUL for the
mismatch period is consistent with the principle that the defaulting entity bears the
financial burden of idle assets, while the subsequent PoC classification ensures
socialisation of costs prospectively.
Analysis and Conclusion
93. While analysing the Issue 1 we had gone through the MOM of various
meetings and also relevant correspondence, and we have already concluded that
it cannot be established that the bays were constructed for use by PTCUL for
connecting downstream transmission lines. The arguments of the PTCUL on the
Issue 5 and response of PGCIL thereon do not add any significant value, and
therefore our conclusion remains unchanged. In regard to specific submission of
PGCIL that subsequent to the amendment to the Sharing Regulations the charges
relatable to bays will be construed as transformer component and will be payable
by UPCL (the distribution licensee in Uttarakhand), we would not like to consider
the same in this judgement, as presently we are only dealing with the issue of
application of transmission charges to PTCUL, which has filed this appeal.

proceedings and later tripartite LTA arrangements, operates as

Our Analysis:
12. At the outset, we may note that Section 114 of CPC is the substantive
provision dealing with scope of review and is quoted below:
“114. Review. —Subject as aforesaid, any person
considering himself aggrieved—
(a) by a decree or order from which an appeal is
____________________________________________________________________________________
RP No.35 of 2025 & batch Page 23 of 39

allowed by this Code, but from which no appeal has
been preferred.
(b) by a decree or order from which no appeal is
allowed by this Code, or
(c) by a decision on a reference from a Court of
Small Causes, may apply for a review of judgment
to the Court which passed the decree or made the
order, and the Court may make such order thereon
as it thinks fit.”
13. The grounds on which review of a judgment / order can be sought,
have been specified in Order XLVII of the CPC which are reproduced
hereinbelow: -
“1. Application for review of judgment. — (1) Any person
considering himself aggrieved—
(a) by a decree or order from which an appeal is
allowed, but from which no appeal has been
preferred,
____________________________________________________________________________________
RP No.35 of 2025 & batch Page 24 of 39

(b) by a decree or order from which no appeal is
allowed, or
(c) by a decision on a reference from a Court of
Small Causes, and who, from the discovery
of new and important matter or evidence which, after
the exercise of due diligence was not within his
knowledge or could not be produced by him at the
time when the decree was passed or order made,
or on account of some mistake or error apparent on
the face of the record or for any other sufficient
reason, desires to obtain a review of the decree
passed or order made against him, may apply
for a review of judgment to the Court which passed
the decree or made the order.
(2) A party who is not appealing from a decree or
order may apply for a review of judgment
notwithstanding the pendency of an appeal by
some other party except where the ground of such
appeal is common to the applicant and the
appellant, or when, being respondent, he can
____________________________________________________________________________________
RP No.35 of 2025 & batch Page 25 of 39

present to the Appellate Court the case on which he
applied for the review.
Explanation.—The fact that the decision on a
question of law on which the judgment of the Court
is based has been reversed or modified by the
subsequent decision of a superior Court in any other
case, shall not be a ground for the review of such
judgment.”
(Emphasis supplied)
14. A bare reading of these relevant legal provisions would make it clear
that an application for review of a judgment / order is maintainable upon (i)
discovery of a new and important matter or evidence which, after exercise of
due diligence, was not within the knowledge of the review applicant or could
not be produced by him when the judgment / order was passed; or (ii) on
account of some mistake or error apparent on the face of record; or (iii) for
any other sufficient reason.
15. The expression “error apparent on the face of record” used in Order
XLVII Rule 1 indicates an error which is self-evident and staring in the eye.
Any error or mistake which is not self-evident and has to be deducted from
____________________________________________________________________________________
RP No.35 of 2025 & batch Page 26 of 39

a process of reasoning cannot be said to be an error apparent on the face of
record justifying exercise of power of review. Power of review can be
exercised only where a glaring omission or a patent mistake is found in the
order under review. We may also note that the power of review can be
exercised only for correction of a patent mistake but not to substitute a view
for the reason that a review petition cannot be permitted to be an appeal in
disguise.
16. In Chhajju Ram v. Neki Ram AIR 1922 PC 112, it was held that the
words “any other sufficient reason” appearing in Order XLVII Rule 1 CPC
must mean “a reason sufficient on grounds at least analogous to those
specified in the rule”. This interpretation was approved by the Supreme Court
in later judgment in Moran Mar Basselios Catholicos v. Most Rev. Mar
Poulose Athanasium 1955 1 SCR 520. In Kamlesh Verma v.
Mayawati & Ors. (2013) 8 SCC 320, Hon’ble Supreme Court has succinctly
summarized the principles for exercising review jurisdiction as under: -
“20. Thus, in view of the above, the following
grounds of review are maintainable as stipulated by
the stature:
20.1 When the review will be maintainable:
(i) Discovery of new and important matter or
____________________________________________________________________________________
RP No.35 of 2025 & batch Page 27 of 39

evidence which, after the exercise of due diligence,
was not within knowledge of the petitioner or could
not be produced by him;
(ii) Mistake or error apparent on the face of the
record;
(iii) Any other sufficient reason.
The words “any other sufficient reason” have been
interpreted in Chhajju Ram v. Neki and approved by
this Court in Moran Mar Basselios Catholicos v.
Most Rev. Mar Poulose Athanasius to mean “a
reason sufficient on grounds at least analogous to
those specified in the rule”. The same principles
have been reiterated in Union of India v. Sandur
manganese & Iron Ores Ltd.
20.2 When the review will not be maintainable:
(i) A repetition of old and overruled argument
is not enough to reopen concluded adjudications.
(ii) Minor mistakes of inconsequential import.
(iii) Review proceedings cannot be equated
with the original hearing of the case.
____________________________________________________________________________________
RP No.35 of 2025 & batch Page 28 of 39

(iv) Review is not maintainable unless the
material error, manifest on the face of the order,
undermines its soundness or results in miscarriage
of justice.
(v) A review is by no means an appeal in
disguise whereby an erroneous decision is reheard
and corrected but lies only for patent error.
(vi) The mere possibility of two views on the
subject cannot be a ground for review.
(vii) The error apparent on the face of the record
should not be an error which has to be fished out
and searched.
(viii) The appreciation of evidence on record is

cannot be permitted to be advanced in the review
petition.

relief sought at the time of arguing the main matter
had been negatived.”

RP No.35 of 2025 & batch Page 29 of 39

17. We also find advantageous to quote here following Paragraphs of the
judgment of the Hon’ble Supreme Court in S. Madhusudhan Reddy v. V.
Narayana Reddy & Ors. (2022) SCC OnLine SC 1034:-
“31. As can be seen from the above exposition of
law, it has been consistently held by this Court in
several judicial pronouncements that the Court’s
jurisdiction of review, is not the same as that of an
appeal. A judgment can be open to review if there
is a mistake or an error apparent on the face of the

Court to exercise its powers of review under

exercising powers of review, the Court can correct a

evidence has emerged after passing of
thejudgment, subject to the condition that such
evidence was not within the knowledge of the party

the order was made despite undertaking an
exercise of due diligence. There is a clear

18. In a recent judgment dated 08.09.2025 passed in Malleeswari v. K.
Suguna and Anr. SLP (C) No. 12787 of 2025 (2025 INSC 1080) Hon'ble
Supreme Court has again reiterated that court’s power to review its own
previous order is strictly limited to correcting errors apparent on the face of
the record and not to rehear or substitute a different view as if it were an
appeal. It has been held in the said judgment that the power of review is
different from appellate power and is subject to the following limitations to
maintain the finality of the judicial decisions:
“15.1 The review proceedings are not by way of an appeal and
have to be strictly confined to the scope and ambit of
Order 47 Rule 1 of CPC.
15.2 Review is not to be confused with appellate powers, which
may enable an appellate court to correct all manner of
errors committed by the subordinate court.
15.3 In exercise of the jurisdiction under Order 47 Rule 1 of
CPC, it is not permissible for an erroneous decision to be
____________________________________________________________________________________
RP No.35 of 2025 & batch Page 32 of 39

reheard and corrected. A review petition, it must be
remembered, has a limited purpose and cannot be
allowed to be an appeal in disguise.
15.4 The power of review can be exercised for the correction
of a mistake, but not to substitute a view. Such powers
can be exercised within the limits specified in the statute
governing the exercise of power.
15.5 The review court does not sit in appeal over its own order.
A rehearing of the matter is impermissible. It constitutes
an exception to the general rule that once a judgment is
signed or pronounced, it should not be altered. Hence, it
is invoked only to prevent a miscarriage of justice or to
correct grave and palpable errors.”
19. Further, after noticing the distinction between power of review and
appellate power, the Hon'ble Supreme Court has succinctly summed up the
grounds of review as under: -
____________________________________________________________________________________
RP No.35 of 2025 & batch Page 33 of 39

“17.1 The ground of discovery of new and important matter or
evidence is a ground available if it is demonstrated that,
despite the exercise of due diligence, this evidence was
not within their knowledge or could not be produced by the
party at the time, the original decree or order was passed.
17.2 Mistake or error apparent on the face of the record may
be invoked if there is something more than a mere error,
and it must be the one which is manifest on the face of the
record. Such an error is a patent error and not a mere
wrong decision. An error which has to be established by a
long-drawn process of reasoning on points where there
may conceivably be two opinions can hardly be said to be
an error apparent on the face of the record.
17.3 Lastly, the phrase 'for any other sufficient reason' means
a reason that is sufficient on grounds at least analogous
to those specified in the other two categories.”
20. We may also note that in the words of Justice Krishna Iyer (as his
Lordship then was), “a plea of review, unless the first judicial view is
____________________________________________________________________________________
RP No.35 of 2025 & batch Page 34 of 39

manifestly distorted, is like asking for the Moon. A forensic defeat cannot be
avenged by an invitation to have a second look, hopeful of discovery of flows
and reversal of result. A review in the counsel’s mentation cannot repair the
verdict once given. So, the law laid down must rest in peace.” (See
Ghanshyam Mishra & Sons (P) Ltd v. Edelweiss Asset Reconstruction Co.

21. Bearing in mind these salutary legal principles governing the power of
a court to review its own decision, let’s now turn to the judgment under review
and the grounds of review raised in these petitions.
22. To state pithily, the issue before this Tribunal was whether the
normative O&M covers the P&G liability of the employees of DVC.
23. The discussion on this issue spans over 12 pages of the judgment from

26. In Paragraph no.179, this Tribunal has held that a harmonious reading
of the statement of reasons as well as Tariff Regulations, 2009 along with
the impugned Tariff Order supports the view taken by the Commission that
contribution made by DVC to P&G Fund is indisputably a manpower related
expenditure which is already allowed to DVC as normative O&M expenses
in terms of these regulations. It has further been held that such a normative
tariff regime would be defeated if a generating company is allowed any O&M
related expenditure by way of additional allowance over and above O&M
norms that are allowed to it in accordance with the tariff regulations.

27. It has been stated that the purpose of norms based tariff scheme is to
incentivize efficiency so that a generating company incurs expenditure
prudently within the prescribed norms.
28. With reference to the reliance placed on behalf of the petitioners on
Regulation 53 read with Section 40 of the DVC Act, it has been observed in
Paragraph no.185 of the judgment that the DVC neither argued nor
established before the Central Commission that P&G Fund had been created
pursuant to the direction/approval of C&AG under Section 40 of the DVC Act.
Even no document in this regard was submitted on behalf of the petitioners
during the course of hearing of these review petitions. It has further been
stated in the said Paragraph that Regulation 53(2)(iv) does not lay down that
an expenditure which is adequately provided for under the O&M norms, has
to be once again allowed as a tariff element.
29. In nutshell, we may note that upon consideration of all the relevant
statutory provisions as well as regulations, this Tribunal has, in the judgment
under review, come to a particular finding on the issue under consideration
which cannot be altered in the review proceedings. A well-reasoned and well
considered judgment, even though erroneous, does not fall within the scope
and ambit of review. There is a clear distinction between a judgment
suffering from error apparent on the face of record and an erroneous

judgment. Review petition is maintainable only in the former case whereas
in the latter case, the remedy available to the aggrieved party is to assail the
order/judgment by way of appeal in the higher forum/court.
30. By way of the instant review petitions, the petitioners are actually
seeking a relook of the judgment under review in the hope to discover any
flaw or fault in the same, which is not permissible in law. The review petitions
manifestly appear to be appeals in disguise and thus, do not fall within the
scope and ambit of Order 47 Rule 1 of the CPC.
31. Hence, we are of the considered opinion that the petitioners have failed
to make out any mistake or error apparent on the face of record in the
judgment under review dated 11.09.2025 and have failed to bring the case
within the parameters laid down by the Hon'ble Supreme Court in various
decisions referred to hereinabove. The review petitions are sans any merit
and are accordingly dismissed.
